concepts.title: Combined pronouns (glielo, me ne, ce lo…)
concepts.rule: Indirect + direct pronoun: mi/ti/ci/vi/si become me/te/ce/ve/se before lo, la, li, le, ne; gli and le (and Lei) both become glie- and fuse into one word (glielo, gliela, glieli, gliele, gliene). In compound tenses the participle agrees with lo/la/li/le and partitive ne: Gliel'ho data.
assessment: Combines indirect and direct object pronouns in the right order and form (me lo, te la, ce li, ve ne)
Uses glielo/gliela/glieli/gliele/gliene for him, her, them and formal you
Makes the past participle agree with lo, la, li, le and partitive ne (Gliel'ho data, Me ne ha date tre)
Elides lo/la before avere (gliel'ho, me l'ha) but never li/le

lesson.intro: English says 'I gave it to him' with two separate words. Italian packs both pronouns into a tight cluster before the verb: *gliel'ho dato*. The forms change when they combine (*mi* → *me*, *gli* → *glie-*), and in compound tenses the participle agrees with the direct pronoun. These clusters are everywhere in spoken Italian, and getting them right instantly sounds fluent.

rules.title: Indirect first, then direct: mi → me, ti → te…
rules.text: When an indirect pronoun (to me, to you…) meets *lo, la, li, le* or *ne*, it comes **first** and its *-i* changes to *-e*: *mi* → **me**, *ti* → **te**, *ci* → **ce**, *vi* → **ve**, *si* → **se**.

examples.it: Mi presti la penna? Sì, **te la** presto.
examples.en: Will you lend me the pen? Yes, I'll lend it to you.

examples.it: Ci mandi le foto? Sì, **ve le** mando stasera.
examples.en: Will you send us the photos? Yes, I'll send them to you tonight.

examples.it: Quanti libri ti ha prestato? **Me ne** ha prestati due.
examples.en: How many books did he lend you? He lent me two.

rules.title: Glie- is the same for him, her, them and Lei
rules.text: *Gli* (to him / to them) and *le* (to her / to you formal) both become **glie-** and join the direct pronoun in **one word**. So *glielo* can mean 'it to him', 'it to her', 'it to them' or 'it to you (Lei)'. Context tells you who. Never write ~~le lo~~ or ~~gli lo~~.

examples.it: Hai dato il regalo a Sara? Sì, **gliel'**ho dato.
examples.en: Did you give Sara the present? Yes, I gave it to her.
Madam, I'll bring you the bill right away.
To the kids? I'll take them to them tomorrow.

rules.title: Participle agreement in compound tenses
rules.text: With *avere*, the past participle agrees with a preceding **lo, la, li, le** and with partitive **ne**, even inside a cluster. *Lo* and *la* elide before *ho, hai, ha, hanno* (*gliel'ho, me l'ha*). *Li* and *le* **never** elide, so the participle ending is the only thing that shows gender.

examples.en: The key? I gave it to him yesterday.
The roses? I gave them to her.

examples.it: Le mele? La nonna **me ne ha date** tre.
examples.en: The apples? Grandma gave me three.

rules.title: Where the cluster goes
rules.text: The cluster goes **before** a conjugated verb (*te lo dico*) and is **attached** to infinitives, gerunds and affirmative tu/noi/voi imperatives (*dirtelo, dicendotelo, dimmelo*). With modal verbs both positions work: *Te lo posso dire / Posso dirtelo*. Positions are covered in depth in B2-PRON-04.

examples.it: Non **te lo** posso spiegare adesso. / Non posso **spiegartelo** adesso.
examples.en: I can't explain it to you now.
Will you give it to me? → Give it to me!

rules.title: Reflexive verbs + direct pronoun
rules.text: Reflexive verbs with an object (*mettersi la giacca, lavarsi le mani*) use the same pattern: *si* → **se**. In compound tenses they take *essere*, and the participle agrees with the direct pronoun: *Le mani? **Me le sono lavate**.*

examples.it: Marco si mette la giacca? Sì, **se la** mette.
examples.en: Is Marco putting his jacket on? Yes, he's putting it on.
My hands? I've already washed them.

mistakes.why: *Le* (to her) becomes *glie-* before *lo*, and it's written as one word.
Before *lo, la, li, le, ne*, *mi* becomes *me*.
The participle agrees with the direct pronoun *la* hidden in *gliel'*: *data*.
Only *lo* and *la* elide. *Le* stays whole: *gliele ho*.
*Gli + lo* fuse into *glielo*, with an extra *-e-*.

tips: When you see *gliel'ho*, look for the noun it replaces: masculine → *dato*, feminine → *data*.
Say the clusters aloud as single words: *melo, tela, glielo, cene*. They are pronounced as one unit with the verb.
*Glielo* is ambiguous on purpose. If you need to be clear, add *a lui / a lei* and use a single pronoun: *L'ho dato a lei, non a lui.*

exercises.prompt: Mi presti la penna? Sì, ___ presto subito.

traps.why: Before *la*, *ti* becomes *te*: *te la*.
The indirect pronoun comes first: *te la*.

exercises.explanation: Indirect (to you) + direct (the pen, feminine): *ti* + *la* → **te la**.
exercises.en: Will you lend me the pen? Yes, I'll lend it to you right away.

exercises.prompt: Quando dai il regalo a Sara? ___ do domani.

traps.why: *Le* (to her) becomes *glie-* before *lo*: *glielo*, one word.
*Gli + lo* fuse into one word with an extra *e*: *glielo*.
Indirect first, and fused: *glielo*.

exercises.explanation: To her (*le*) + it (*lo*, il regalo) → **glielo**. *Glie-* is used for him, her and them alike.
exercises.en: When are you giving Sara the present? I'm giving it to her tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Porti i documenti ai signori Rossi? Sì, ___ porto stasera.

traps.why: *Gli + li* → *glieli*, written as one word.
Indirect pronoun first, fused: *glieli*.
*I documenti* is masculine plural, so the direct part is *li*: *glieli*.

exercises.en: Are you taking the documents to Mr and Mrs Rossi? Yes, I'm taking them tonight.

exercises.instruction: Complete with a combined pronoun. Careful with the point of view!
exercises.prompt: Ci mandi le foto del matrimonio? Sì, ___ mando stasera.

traps.why: They asked 'will you send *us*'. You answer 'I'll send them to *you* (plural)': *ve le*.
Before *le*, *vi* becomes *ve*: *ve le*.
*Le foto* is feminine plural (*la foto*, short for *fotografia*): *ve le*.

exercises.explanation: To you plural (*vi*) + them (*le*, le foto) → **ve le**.
exercises.en: Will you send us the wedding photos? Yes, I'll send them to you tonight.

exercises.instruction: Answer with a combined pronoun and the passato prossimo of the verb in brackets.
exercises.prompt: Hai restituito la bici a Paolo? Sì, ___ (restituire) ieri.

traps.why: *Gliel'* hides *la* (la bici), so the participle agrees: *restituita*.
*Gli + la* → *gliela*, which elides to *gliel'ho*: one word.
You also need 'to him': *gliel'ho restituita*.

exercises.explanation: To him (*gli*) + it (*la*, la bici) → *gliela* → **gliel'ho**. The participle agrees with *la*: **restituita**.
exercises.en: Did you give the bike back to Paolo? Yes, I gave it back to him yesterday.

exercises.instruction: Choose the correct form. The waiter is speaking formally (Lei).
exercises.prompt: Signora, il conto? ___ porto subito.

optionWhy.2: Indirect comes first and the two fuse: *glielo*.
optionWhy.3: *Gli + lo* is written as one word with an extra *e*: *glielo*.

exercises.en: Madam, the bill? I'll bring it to you right away.

exercises.instruction: Answer with a combined pronoun and the passato prossimo of the verb in brackets.
exercises.prompt: Quante mele ti ha dato la nonna? ___ (dare) tre.

traps.why: In careful Italian the participle agrees with partitive *ne*, which stands for *mele* (feminine plural): *date*. *Dato* is common in speech but marked.
Before *ne*, *mi* becomes *me*: *me ne*.
*Mele* is feminine: *date*.
With a number and no noun you need *ne*: *me ne ha date tre*.

exercises.explanation: To me (*mi* → *me*) + of them (*ne*) → **me ne**. The participle agrees with *ne* = *mele*: **date**.
exercises.en: How many apples did Grandma give you? She gave me three.

exercises.instruction: Replace both objects (il pacco, a mia sorella) with a combined pronoun.
exercises.prompt: Ho spedito il pacco a mia sorella.

traps.why: *Le* (to her) becomes *glie-* in a cluster: *gliel'ho*.
The participle agrees with the direct object, *il pacco* (masculine): *spedito*. Not with the sister.
One word: *gliel'ho*.

exercises.explanation: *A mia sorella* → *le*; *il pacco* → *lo*. *Le + lo* → *glielo*, elided before *ho*: **Gliel'ho spedito**.
exercises.en: I sent it to her.

exercises.instruction: Replace both objects (le rose, a mia madre) with a combined pronoun.
exercises.prompt: Ho regalato le rose a mia madre.

traps.why: The participle agrees with *le* (le rose): *regalate*.
Only *lo* and *la* elide. *Le* never does: *gliele ho*.
*Le* (to her) becomes *glie-*: *gliele*.

exercises.explanation: To her + them (fem. pl.) → **gliele**, no elision, and the participle agrees: **regalate**.
exercises.en: I gave them to her.

exercises.prompt: I'll tell you about it later.

traps.why: Before *ne*, *ti* becomes *te*: *te ne parlo*.
*Parlare **di** qualcosa*: 'about it' = *ne*, not *lo*.

exercises.explanation: *Parlare di* → 'about it' is *ne*. To you (*ti*) + *ne* → **te ne**.
exercises.en: I'll tell you about it later.

exercises.instruction: Translate into Italian. 'The keys' = le chiavi; 'him' = Marco.
exercises.prompt: Yes, I gave them to him yesterday.

traps.why: The participle agrees with *le* (le chiavi, feminine plural): *date*.
*Le chiavi* is feminine: *gliele*.
*Le* doesn't elide: *gliele ho*.

exercises.explanation: To him + them (fem. pl.) → **gliele ho**, and the participle agrees: **date**.
exercises.en: Yes, I gave them to him yesterday.

exercises.prompt: Can you repeat it for me?
exercises.explanation: With a modal, the cluster can go before the modal: **Me lo** puoi ripetere (or attached: *Puoi ripetermelo*).

exercises.prompt: Your colleague asks whether you've sent the report (la relazione) to the director. Say yes, you sent it to him this morning.

traps.why: *Gliel'* contains *la* (la relazione): the participle must be feminine, *mandata*.
You need 'to him' as well: *gliel'ho*.

exercises.en: Yes, I sent it to him this morning.

exercises.prompt: Che belle scarpe! Chi ___ ha regalate?

optionWhy.2: *Scarpe* is feminine, and *regalate* confirms it: *te le*.

exercises.explanation: To you (*ti* → *te*) + them (*le*, le scarpe) → **te le**. The participle *regalate* agrees with *le*.
exercises.en: What lovely shoes! Who gave them to you?

exercises.prompt: Marco si mette la cravatta per il colloquio? Sì, ___ mette.

traps.why: Before *la*, reflexive *si* becomes *se*: *se la*.
He's putting it on *himself*: reflexive *se la*, not *gliela* (to him, someone else).
*Mettersi* is reflexive, so keep the reflexive part: *se la mette*.

exercises.en: Is Marco wearing a tie for the interview? Yes, he is.

exercises.instruction: Replace both objects (i soldi, a Giulia e a Marco) with pronouns.
exercises.prompt: Non ho ancora restituito i soldi a Giulia e a Marco.

traps.match: Non li ho ancora restituiti loro
traps.why: Correct but formal: *loro* after the verb. In everyday Italian *glieli* is the norm.
The participle agrees with *li* (i soldi): *restituiti*.

traps.match: Non gli li ho ancora restituiti
traps.why: One word: *glieli*.

traps.match: Non le li ho ancora restituiti
traps.why: For a mixed group ('to them') use *gli* → *glieli*.

exercises.explanation: To them (*gli*) + them (*li*) → **glieli**, before the verb; the participle agrees: **restituiti**.
exercises.en: I haven't given it back to them yet.

exercises.instruction: Translate into Italian ('it' = something she explained, masculine).
exercises.prompt: She's already explained it to me twice.
answers: (Me l'ha|Me lo ha) già spiegato due volte
[Lei] (me l'ha|me lo ha) già spiegato due volte

traps.why: Before *lo*, *mi* becomes *me*: *me l'ha*.
*Spiegare* takes *avere*: *me l'ha spiegato*.

exercises.explanation: To me (*mi* → *me*) + it (*lo*, elided) → **me l'ha** spiegato.
exercises.en: She's already explained it to me twice.

concepts.title: Ci and ne in depth
concepts.rule: Ne replaces di + something and quantities (Ne voglio due; Che ne pensi?); ci replaces a/in/su + something or a place (Ci vado; Ci penso io). With essere: ce n'è / ce ne sono. Pensarci = think about it; pensarne = have an opinion of it.
assessment: Uses partitive ne with numbers and quantities, including participle agreement (Ne ho mangiate due)
Uses ne for di + thing (parlarne, averne bisogno, che ne pensi)
Uses ci for places and a/in/su + thing (andarci, pensarci, crederci, riuscirci)
Produces c'è / ci sono vs ce n'è / ce ne sono correctly

lesson.intro: English often leaves these words out: 'How many do you have? I have two.' Italian can't: *Ne ho due.* And many verbs that take *a* or *di* need *ci* or *ne* to say 'about it', 'to it' or 'there'. Missing *ci* and *ne* is one of the most noticeable traits of foreign Italian, and using them well sounds immediately native.

rules.title: Partitive ne: quantities
rules.text: When you mention a number or quantity without repeating the noun, you need **ne** ('of them / of it'): *Ne ho due, Ne voglio un po', Non ne ho*. In compound tenses the participle agrees with the noun *ne* stands for.

examples.en: How many brothers do you have? I have two.

examples.it: Vuoi del vino? Sì, **ne** prendo un bicchiere.
examples.en: Want some wine? Yes, I'll have a glass.
The pizzas? We ate four.

rules.title: Ne = di + something
rules.text: Verbs and expressions with *di* use **ne** for 'of/about it': *parlarne* (parlare di), *averne bisogno* (aver bisogno di), *esserne sicuro* (essere sicuro di), *che ne pensi?* (pensare di = opinion), *ricordarsene*, *occuparsene*.

examples.en: Let's talk about it tomorrow.
I don't need it.
What do you think of the film?

rules.title: Ci = a / in / su + something, or 'there'
rules.text: **Ci** replaces a place (*Ci vado domani*) and *a/in/su* + a thing: *pensarci* (pensare a), *crederci* (credere a), *riuscirci* (riuscire a), *contarci* (contare su), *provarci* (provare a). *Ci penso io* = I'll take care of it.

examples.it: Vai spesso a Roma? Sì, **ci** vado ogni mese.
examples.en: Do you often go to Rome? Yes, I go there every month.
I don't believe it!

examples.it: Hai pensato al regalo? Sì, **ci** ho pensato.
examples.en: Have you thought about the present? Yes, I have.

rules.title: C'è / ci sono vs ce n'è / ce ne sono
rules.text: *C'è* and *ci sono* = there is / there are. When you give a quantity without the noun, add **ne**: *ci* → *ce*, giving **ce n'è** (singular) and **ce ne sono** (plural).

rules.title: Pensarci vs pensarne, parlarne, crederci
rules.text: *Pensare a* (think about, take care of) → **ci**: *Ci penso io.* *Pensare di* (have an opinion of) → **ne**: *Che ne pensi?* Many verbs need one or the other: learn them with their preposition.

head: Verb + prep.
With pronoun
Meaning
rows: think about it / see to it

mistakes.why: A number without its noun needs partitive *ne*.
'What do you think of it?' is naturally *Che ne pensi?* (*pensare di* → *ne*).
'There are two (of them)': add *ne*, and *ci* becomes *ce*.

mistakes.wrong: Le pizze? Ne ho mangiato tre.
mistakes.why: The participle agrees with what *ne* refers to (pizze, fem. pl.).
'I'll take care of it' is *pensare a* → *ci*.

tips: Ask yourself which preposition the verb takes: *a/in/su* → *ci*; *di/da* or a quantity → *ne*.
*Ce n'è* and *ce ne sono* are pronounced as one word: *cenè, cenesòno*.
*Ci penso io!* and *Non ci credo!* are high-frequency spoken chunks. Learn them whole.

exercises.prompt: Quanti fratelli hai? ___ ho due.

traps.why: With a number, use partitive *ne* ('of them'): *Ne ho due*.
*Ci* is for places and *a* + thing. For quantities use *ne*.

exercises.en: How many brothers do you have? I have two.

exercises.prompt: Vai spesso a Roma? Sì, ___ vado ogni mese.

traps.why: 'There' (to a place) is *ci*: *ci vado*.

exercises.en: Do you often go to Rome? Yes, I go there every month.

exercises.prompt: Hai bisogno della macchina? No, non ___ ho bisogno.

traps.why: *Avere bisogno **di*** → *ne*.
*Bisogno di* takes *ne*, not a direct object pronoun.

exercises.en: Do you need the car? No, I don't need it.

exercises.prompt: C'è ancora del latte? Sì, ___ ancora un po'.

traps.why: With a quantity (*un po'*) and no noun, add *ne*: *ce n'è*.
Before *ne*, *ci* becomes *ce*: *ce n'è*.

exercises.en: Is there any milk left? Yes, there's still a bit.

exercises.prompt: Quante persone ci sono in sala? ___ almeno cinquanta.

traps.why: A number without its noun needs *ne*: *ce ne sono*.
*Ci* becomes *ce* before *ne*.
'There are' still needs *ci*: *ce ne sono*.

exercises.explanation: There are (*ci sono*) + of them (*ne*) → **ce ne sono**.
exercises.en: How many people are in the hall? There are at least fifty.

exercises.prompt: Hai pensato al regalo per la mamma? Sì, ___ ho pensato ieri.

optionWhy.2: *Pensare a qualcosa* isn't a direct object: use *ci*.
optionWhy.3: *Gli* is for people ('to him'). For a thing after *a*, use *ci*.

exercises.en: Have you thought about Mum's present? Yes, I thought about it yesterday.

exercises.prompt: Che ___ pensi del nuovo sindaco?

optionWhy.1: Asking for an opinion is *pensare **di*** → *ne*. *Pensarci* means 'think about / see to it'.

exercises.en: What do you think of the new mayor?

exercises.instruction: Answer using ne and the passato prossimo of the verb in brackets.
exercises.prompt: Quante pizze avete mangiato? ___ (mangiare) quattro.

traps.why: In careful Italian the participle agrees with *ne* (= pizze, feminine plural): *mangiate*.
A number without the noun needs *ne*: *Ne abbiamo mangiate quattro*.
With a quantity, use partitive *ne*, not *le*.

exercises.explanation: Partitive **ne** + participle agreeing with *pizze*: **ne abbiamo mangiate** quattro.
exercises.en: How many pizzas did you eat? We ate four.

exercises.instruction: Replace 'a questa storia' with ci or ne.
exercises.prompt: Non credo a questa storia.

traps.why: *Credere **a*** → *ci*.
*Credere a qualcosa* isn't a direct object: *Non ci credo*.

exercises.en: I don't believe it.

exercises.instruction: Replace 'di questo problema' with ci or ne.
exercises.prompt: Parliamo di questo problema domani.

traps.why: *Ci parliamo* means 'we'll talk to each other'. 'About it' = *parlare di* → *ne*.
*Parlare di* → *ne*, not *lo*.

exercises.en: Let's talk about it tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: I'll take care of it.

traps.why: 'I'll take care of it' = *pensarci*: *Ci penso io*.
*Pensare a* (see to) → *ci*: *Ci penso io*.

exercises.explanation: *Pensare a* = see to something → **Ci penso io**. Also *Me ne occupo (io)* (*occuparsi di* → *ne*).
exercises.en: I'll take care of it.

exercises.instruction: Translate the answer into Italian. Question: 'Quanti studenti ci sono nella classe?'
exercises.prompt: There are twenty.

traps.why: Without the noun you need *ne*: *Ce ne sono venti*.
*Ci* becomes *ce* before *ne*.
Also possible ('They are twenty'), but *Ce ne sono venti* answers the question exactly.

exercises.explanation: *Ci sono* + quantity without noun → **ce ne sono**.
exercises.en: There are twenty (of them).

exercises.prompt: There isn't any left.
exercises.explanation: *Non* + **ce n'è** + *più*: the cluster stays together before the verb.

exercises.prompt: A friend invites you to Giulia's party. Say: 'I'll think about it.'

traps.why: *Pensare a* (think about) → *ci*. *Ne* would ask for an opinion.
'Think about it' = *pensarci*, not *pensarlo*.

exercises.en: I'll think about it.

exercises.prompt: Sei riuscito ad aprire la porta? No, non ___ sono riuscito.

traps.why: *Riuscire **a*** → *ci*: *non ci sono riuscito*.
*Riuscire a fare qualcosa* → *riuscirci*, not *lo*.

exercises.en: Did you manage to open the door? No, I didn't manage it.

exercises.prompt: Ti ricordi di quel ristorante a Napoli? Sì, me ___ ricordo benissimo.

optionWhy.3: The reflexive is already there (*me*). The gap needs *ne* for 'of it'.

exercises.en: Do you remember that restaurant in Naples? Yes, I remember it very well.

exercises.instruction: Translate the answer into Italian. Question: 'Hai parlato a Laura del problema?'
exercises.prompt: No, I haven't talked to her about it yet.
answers: No, non gliene ho ancora parlato
No, ancora non gliene ho parlato

traps.why: *Le* (to her) + *ne* → *gliene*, one word.
*Parlare di* → *ne*. 'To her' + 'about it' → *gliene*.
*Gli + ne* fuse into *gliene*.

exercises.en: No, I haven't talked to her about it yet.

concepts.title: Pronominal verbs (andarsene, farcela, cavarsela, prendersela…)
concepts.rule: Pronominal verbs carry fixed pronouns that change their meaning (andarsene = leave, farcela = manage, cavarsela = get by, prendersela = take offence, metterci = take time). The reflexive part conjugates (me ne vado, te la prendi), and compound tenses follow the pronouns: ce l'ho fatta, me ne sono andato, me la sono presa.
assessment: Conjugates andarsene, cavarsela, prendersela, sentirsela in the present (me ne vado, te la cavi…)
Chooses metterci (personal) vs volerci (impersonal, agrees with the noun)
Forms compound tenses with the right auxiliary and agreement (ce l'ho fatta, se n'è andato, me la sono presa)
Uses imperatives such as vattene, smettila, finitela, non te la prendere

lesson.intro: *Me ne vado*, *ce l'ho fatta*, *non te la prendere*: these verbs are all over spoken Italian, and they are where learners stop sounding like textbooks. The pronouns are frozen parts of the verb with idiomatic meanings ('it' in *farcela* doesn't refer to anything). You learn each verb as a unit, then conjugate the reflexive part.

rules.title: Andarsene: leave, go away
rules.text: *Andarsene* = *andare* + *si* + *ne*. The reflexive pronoun changes with the person, *ne* stays: **me ne vado, te ne vai, se ne va, ce ne andiamo, ve ne andate, se ne vanno**. Compound tenses use *essere*: *me ne sono andato/a*. Imperative: *vattene! andatevene! non te ne andare / non andartene*.

examples.en: It's late, I'm off.
Luca left without saying goodbye.
Go away!

rules.title: The -sela verbs
rules.text: The *la* in these verbs refers to nothing in particular. The reflexive part conjugates: *me la cavo, te la cavi, se la cava…*

head: Infinitive
Present (io)
Passato prossimo (io)
Meaning
rows: to be angry with, have it in for
to stop it, cut it out

rules.title: Compound tenses: follow the pronouns
rules.text: If the verb contains a **reflexive** pronoun (*me, te, se…*), it takes **essere**: *me la sono cavata, se n'è andata*. If it has only *ci* + *la* (*farcela, avercela*) it takes **avere**. Either way the participle agrees with **la**: *ce l'ho fatt**a***, *me la sono pres**a***.

examples.en: I finally made it!

examples.it: Giulia **se l'è presa** per la battuta.
examples.en: Giulia was offended by the joke.
I got through the exam.

rules.title: Metterci vs volerci: 'it takes'
rules.text: **Metterci** has a personal subject (who or what takes the time) and conjugates normally: *Ci metto un'ora, Il treno ci mette due ore*. **Volerci** is impersonal and agrees with the time or thing needed: *Ci vuole un'ora, Ci vogliono due ore*. In compound tenses: *ci ho messo* (avere) but *ci è voluta un'ora / ci sono volute due ore* (essere, agreement).

examples.en: How long does it take you to get there?

examples.it: **Ci vogliono** tre ore da Roma a Napoli in macchina.
examples.en: It takes three hours from Rome to Naples by car.
It took an hour and a half.

rules.title: Imperatives
rules.text: Affirmative tu/voi: pronouns attached: *vattene, andatevene, smettila, finitela, cavatela*. Negative tu: *non te ne andare / non andartene, non te la prendere / non prendertela*.

examples.en: Stop complaining!
Don't be offended, I was joking.

mistakes.why: Before *ne*, *mi* becomes *me*.
*Volerci* agrees with what's needed: plural *ore* → *vogliono*.

mistakes.wrong: Io ci vuole un'ora per arrivare.
mistakes.why: With a personal subject use *metterci*.
The participle agrees with the hidden *la*.
*Prendersela* is reflexive, so it takes *essere*.

tips: Learn these as chunks: *ce la faccio / ce l'ho fatta*, *me la cavo*, *non me la sento*.
*Ce l'ho con te* (I'm angry with you) looks like *ce l'ho* (I've got it). Context decides.
*Prendersela* is about taking offence; *offendersi* means the same and is safe in writing.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the present tense of the verb in brackets.
exercises.prompt: È tardi, io ___ (andarsene).

traps.why: Before *ne*, *mi* becomes *me*: *me ne vado*.
*Vado* alone means 'I go'. 'I'm leaving' is *me ne vado*.
Reflexive first: *me ne vado*.

exercises.en: It's late, I'm leaving.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the present tense of 'fare'.
exercises.prompt: È difficile, ma insieme ce la ___ (fare, noi).

traps.why: Double *c*: *facciamo*.

exercises.explanation: *Farcela* (noi) → **ce la facciamo** = we can do it.
exercises.en: It's difficult, but together we can do it.

exercises.prompt: Per arrivare a Milano in treno ___ almeno tre ore.

optionWhy.1: *Volerci* agrees with what's needed: *tre ore* (plural) → *ci vogliono*.
optionWhy.2: *Metterci* needs a personal subject (*il treno ci mette*). Here there is none.

exercises.en: It takes at least three hours to get to Milan by train.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the present tense of the verb in brackets (subject: tu).
exercises.prompt: Quanto tempo ___ (metterci) per arrivare in ufficio?

traps.why: *Ci vuole* is impersonal. The cue gives the subject *tu*, so use *metterci*: *ci metti*.
*Metterci* needs *ci*: *ci metti*.

exercises.en: How long does it take you to get to the office?

exercises.instruction: Complete with the negative tu imperative of 'prendersela'.
exercises.prompt: Non ___, stavo solo scherzando!

traps.why: Keep the reflexive part: *non prendertela* / *non te la prendere*.
Before *la*, *ti* becomes *te*.
The negative tu imperative uses the infinitive: *non te la prendere*.

exercises.explanation: Negative tu imperative = *non* + infinitive: **non te la prendere** or **non prendertela**.
exercises.en: Don't be offended, I was only joking!

exercises.instruction: Complete with the passato prossimo of 'farcela' (io).
exercises.prompt: Ho superato l'esame: alla fine ___!

traps.why: The participle agrees with the hidden *la*: *fatta*, whoever is speaking.
*Farcela* has no reflexive pronoun, so it takes *avere*: *ce l'ho fatta*.

exercises.en: I passed the exam: I made it in the end!

exercises.instruction: Complete with the passato prossimo of 'andarsene'.
exercises.prompt: Ieri Luca ___ senza salutare nessuno.

traps.why: *Andarsene* takes *essere*: *se n'è andato*.
*Andarsene* needs *ne*: *se n'è andato*.
*È andato* = he went. 'He left' is *se n'è andato*.

exercises.en: Yesterday Luca left without saying goodbye to anyone.

exercises.prompt: Perché ___ con me? Non ti ho fatto niente!

optionWhy.3: *Farcela* means 'to manage'. Being angry with someone is *avercela con*.

exercises.explanation: *Avercela con qualcuno* = to be angry with someone: **ce l'hai** con me.
exercises.en: Why are you angry with me? I haven't done anything to you!

exercises.instruction: Complete with the present tense of 'cavarsela' (io).
exercises.prompt: Come va con il nuovo lavoro? Mah, ___.

traps.why: Before *la*, *mi* becomes *me*.
*Cavarsela* keeps *la*: *me la cavo*.

exercises.en: How's the new job going? Well, I'm getting by.

exercises.prompt: Giulia se la prende per la critica.
answers: Giulia se l'è presa per la critica
Giulia se la è presa per la critica

traps.why: The participle agrees with *la*: *presa*.
*Prendersela* is reflexive, so it takes *essere*: *se l'è presa*.

exercises.en: Giulia was offended by the criticism.

exercises.prompt: It took me two hours to finish.
answers: Ci ho messo due ore (a|per) finire
Mi ci sono volute due ore (a|per) finire

traps.why: *Volerci* agrees with *due ore*: *ci sono volute*. Or use *ci ho messo*.
A finished action: passato prossimo, *ci ho messo* / *ci sono volute*.

match: Mi ha preso due ore (a|per) finire
traps.why: Calque of 'it took'. Italian uses *metterci* or *volerci*.

exercises.explanation: Personal: **Ci ho messo** due ore. Impersonal: *Mi ci sono volute due ore*.
exercises.en: It took me two hours to finish.

exercises.prompt: I don't feel up to driving tonight.
answers: Non me la sento di guidare stasera
Stasera non me la sento di guidare

traps.why: *Sentirsela*: *non me la sento*.
*Sentirsela **di*** + infinitive.

exercises.explanation: *Sentirsela di* = to feel up to: **Non me la sento di** guidare.
exercises.en: I don't feel up to driving tonight.

exercises.instruction: Put the words in order to tell a friend to stop complaining.
exercises.prompt: Stop complaining!
exercises.explanation: *Smetterla di* + infinitive. Pronouns attach to the tu imperative: **Smettila**, and to the infinitive: *lamentarti*.

exercises.prompt: You and your partner are tired and want to leave a party. Tell your friends: 'We're leaving.'

traps.why: Before *ne*, *ci* becomes *ce*: *ce ne andiamo*.
*Andiamo* = let's go / we're going (somewhere). 'We're leaving' is *ce ne andiamo*.

exercises.en: We're leaving.

exercises.prompt: Ieri, con il traffico, ___ un'ora e mezza per tornare a casa.

optionWhy.3: *Un'ora e mezza* is singular (the head noun is *un'ora*).

exercises.en: Yesterday, with the traffic, it took an hour and a half to get home.

exercises.prompt: Sono arrabbiato con il mio capo.

traps.why: *Avercela* keeps *ci*: *ce l'ho con*.

traps.match: Ce la ho (con il|col) mio capo
traps.why: *La* elides before *ho*: *ce l'ho*.

exercises.explanation: *Avercela con qualcuno* (io) → **Ce l'ho con** il mio capo.
exercises.en: I'm angry with my boss.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the voi imperative of 'finirla'.
exercises.prompt: Ragazzi, ___ di urlare! Il bambino dorme.

traps.why: *Finiscila* is the tu form. You're talking to *ragazzi* (voi): *finitela*.
In the affirmative imperative the pronoun is attached: *finitela*.

exercises.en: Kids, stop shouting! The baby's sleeping.

concepts.title: Pronoun position with infinitives, gerunds, imperatives and modals
concepts.rule: Pronouns go before a conjugated verb but attach to infinitives, gerunds and affirmative tu/noi/voi imperatives (dirlo, dicendolo, dimmelo). With modals both positions work (Lo posso fare / Posso farlo). Negative tu: non dirmelo or non me lo dire. Lei imperative: before (Me lo dia). Da', di', fa', sta', va' double the consonant (dammi, dimmi, fallo), except before gli (digli).
assessment: Attaches pronouns to infinitives and gerunds (cercare di farlo, leggendolo)
Uses both positions with modal verbs and never places pronouns between modal and infinitive
Forms affirmative and negative imperatives with pronouns (dammelo, non dirmelo / non me lo dire, me lo dia)
Doubles the consonant with monosyllabic imperatives (dimmi, fallo, vacci) but not with gli (digli)

lesson.intro: In English, 'it' always comes after the verb. In Italian, the pronoun moves: before a conjugated verb, but glued to the end of infinitives, gerunds and most imperatives. The imperative is the trickiest, because the formal *Lei* form and negative forms behave differently. Mastering this is what makes commands and requests sound natural.

rules.title: Conjugated verb: before
rules.text: With any conjugated verb (indicative, subjunctive, conditional) the pronoun goes **before**, after *non*: *Lo vedo. Non lo vedo. Te lo direi.*

examples.en: I'm not telling you.
If I knew, I'd tell you.

rules.title: Infinitive, gerund, ecco: attached
rules.text: Infinitives drop the final *-e* and take the pronoun at the end: *vedere* → *veder**lo***, *dire* → *dir**telo***. Gerunds: *vedendo**lo***. Also *ecco*: *ecco**lo***, *ecco**mi***. This includes infinitives after non-modal verbs: *Ho cercato di farlo* (never ~~l'ho cercato di fare~~).

examples.en: It's important to tell him right away.
Reading it, I understood everything.
Where's Marco? Here he is!

rules.title: Modals: two positions
rules.text: With *potere, dovere, volere* (and *sapere* = be able) the pronoun goes **either before the modal or attached to the infinitive**: *Lo voglio vedere* = *Voglio vederlo*. Never in between: ~~Voglio lo vedere~~. In compound tenses, the position affects the auxiliary: *Sono dovuto andarci* / *Ci sono dovuto andare*.

examples.en: I can explain it to you.
I don't want to go there.

rules.title: Imperatives
rules.text: Affirmative **tu, noi, voi**: attached (*dammelo, diciamoglielo, fatelo*). Formal **Lei** (and Loro): before (*Me lo dia, Si accomodi*). Negative **tu** = *non* + infinitive, pronoun before or attached: *Non dirmelo / Non me lo dire*. Negative noi/voi: *Non fatelo / Non lo fate*.

head: Affirmative
Negative
rows: Non dirmelo! / Non me lo dire!
Non ditemelo! / Non me lo dite!

rules.title: Da', di', fa', sta', va': double the consonant
rules.text: These one-syllable tu imperatives double the first consonant of the pronoun: *da' + mi* → **dammi**, *di' + lo* → **dillo**, *fa' + lo* → **fallo**, *va' + ci* → **vacci**, *sta' + mi a sentire* → **stammi** a sentire. Exception: **gli** never doubles: **digli, dagli, fagli**.

examples.en: Tell me the truth!
Do it right away!
Tell him to call me.

mistakes.why: Before the modal or attached to the infinitive, never in between.

mistakes.right: Non dirmelo! / Non me lo dire!
mistakes.why: The negative tu imperative uses the infinitive.
*Da'* + *mi* doubles the consonant: *dammi*.
With the Lei imperative the pronouns go before the verb.
*Gli* is the one pronoun that never doubles.

tips: For negative commands to a friend, *Non me lo dire!* is a bit more colloquial and *Non dirmelo!* a bit neater. Both are correct.
If in doubt with a modal, attach to the infinitive: *Posso farlo* is always right.
Stress doesn't move when you add pronouns: *DImmelo, porTAteglielo*.

exercises.prompt: Questo libro è bellissimo: devi ___ (leggere + lo)!

traps.why: Not between modal and infinitive. Attach it: *devi leggerlo* (or *lo devi leggere*).
The infinitive drops its final *-e*: *leggerlo*.

exercises.explanation: Attached to the infinitive, which loses its *-e*: **leggerlo**.
exercises.en: This book is wonderful: you must read it!

exercises.instruction: Move the pronoun to the other possible position.
exercises.prompt: Ti voglio dire una cosa.

traps.why: Never between modal and infinitive: *Voglio dirti*.
The infinitive loses its *-e*: *dirti*.

exercises.explanation: With modals: before the modal (*Ti voglio dire*) or attached to the infinitive (**Voglio dirti**).
exercises.en: I want to tell you something.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the tu imperative of 'dire' + 'mi'.
exercises.prompt: ___ la verità!

traps.why: *Di'* + *mi* doubles the *m*: *dimmi*.
Affirmative tu imperative: the pronoun is attached: *dimmi*.

exercises.en: Tell me the truth!

exercises.instruction: Complete with the tu imperative of 'dare' + 'me' + 'lo'.
exercises.prompt: Il telecomando? ___ subito!

traps.why: *Da'* doubles the consonant: *dammelo*.
In a cluster *mi* becomes *me*: *dammelo*.
That's a question/statement. The command attaches the pronouns: *dammelo*.

exercises.en: The remote? Give it to me right now!

exercises.prompt: Dimmelo!

traps.why: Negative tu imperative = *non* + infinitive: *non dirmelo* / *non me lo dire*.
*Mi* becomes *me* before *lo*.

exercises.explanation: Negative tu = *non* + infinitive: **Non dirmelo** or **Non me lo dire**.
exercises.en: Don't tell me!

exercises.instruction: You're speaking formally to an older lady (Lei). Choose the correct form.
exercises.prompt: Signora, ___ un momento, per favore.

optionWhy.1: With the Lei imperative the pronoun goes before: *mi ascolti*.
optionWhy.2: *Ascolta* is the indicative ('she listens to me').
optionWhy.3: *Ascoltami* is the tu form: too familiar here.

exercises.explanation: Lei imperative (= present subjunctive) with the pronoun **before**: **mi ascolti**.
exercises.en: Madam, listen to me for a moment, please.

exercises.prompt: Ho cercato di ___ (convincere + lo), ma non c'è stato niente da fare.

traps.why: After *di*, the infinitive takes the pronoun at the end: *convincerlo*.

exercises.explanation: *Cercare di* isn't a modal: the pronoun can only attach to the infinitive: **convincerlo**.
exercises.en: I tried to persuade him, but there was nothing doing.

exercises.prompt: 'I can do it' / 'I can't do it'

optionWhy.0: This one is correct: pronoun before the modal.
optionWhy.1: This one is correct: pronoun attached to the infinitive.
optionWhy.3: This one is correct: *non* + pronoun + modal.

exercises.explanation: The pronoun can't sit between the modal and the infinitive: ~~Posso lo fare~~ is the wrong one.
exercises.en: I can do it.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the voi imperative of 'mangiare' + 'la'.
exercises.prompt: Ragazzi, la torta è pronta: ___ finché è calda!

traps.why: Affirmative voi imperative: attach the pronoun: *mangiatela*.
*Mangiala* is tu. You're talking to *ragazzi*: *mangiatela*.

exercises.en: Guys, the cake's ready: eat it while it's warm!

exercises.prompt: Do it now!

traps.why: *Fa'* + *lo* doubles the *l*: *fallo*.
Attach the pronoun and double the consonant: *fallo*.
That's a statement. The command is *Fallo*.

exercises.en: Do it now!

exercises.prompt: I can't explain it to you now.

traps.why: Before *lo*, *ti* becomes *te*: *te lo* / *spiegartelo*.
Not between modal and infinitive: *Non te lo posso spiegare* or *Non posso spiegartelo*.

exercises.explanation: Modal: **Non te lo posso spiegare** or **Non posso spiegartelo**.
exercises.en: I can't explain it to you now.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite the first part using a gerund.
exercises.prompt: Mentre lo leggevo, ho capito tutto.

traps.why: Pronouns attach to the gerund: *leggendolo*.

exercises.en: Reading it, I understood everything.

exercises.prompt: I have to tell you (it).
exercises.explanation: The cluster goes before the modal (**Te lo devo dire**) or attaches to the infinitive (*Devo dirtelo*).

exercises.instruction: Say it aloud (or type). Use a pronoun for 'the salt'.
exercises.prompt: At dinner, ask a friend to pass you the salt: 'Pass it to me, please.'

traps.why: One cluster, with *mi* → *me*: *passamelo*.
*Da'* doubles the consonant: *dammelo*.

exercises.explanation: Tu imperative + *me lo*: **Passamelo** (or the question *Me lo passi?*).
exercises.en: Pass it to me, please.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the Lei imperative of 'dare' + 'me' + 'lo'.
exercises.prompt: Signor Bianchi, il contratto firmato ___ domani, per cortesia.

traps.why: *Dammelo* is tu. With *Signor Bianchi* use Lei: *me lo dia*.
*Mi* becomes *me* before *lo*.
With the Lei imperative both pronouns go before: *me lo dia*.
*Dà* is the indicative. The Lei imperative is *dia*.

exercises.explanation: Lei imperative (*dia*) with pronouns **before**: **me lo dia**.
exercises.en: Mr Bianchi, please give me the signed contract tomorrow.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the tu imperative of 'dire' + 'gli'.
exercises.prompt: Vai da Luca e ___ di chiamarmi stasera.

traps.why: *Gli* is the exception: it never doubles. *Digli*.
Affirmative tu imperative: attach: *digli*.
*Dille* = tell *her*. Luca is a man: *digli*.

exercises.en: Go to Luca and tell him to call me tonight.

exercises.instruction: Translate into Italian (noi imperative; 'her' = Anna, 'it' = il segreto).
exercises.prompt: Let's tell her right away!

traps.why: Correct as a statement ('we'll tell her right away'). As a command, attach: *diciamoglielo*.
*Il segreto* is masculine: *-lo*, so *diciamoglielo*.
*Le* (to her) becomes *glie-* in a cluster, and everything attaches: *diciamoglielo*.

exercises.en: Let's tell her right away!

concepts.title: Relative pronouns: cui, il quale, chi, ciò che
concepts.rule: Che for subjects and direct objects; preposition + cui after any preposition (di cui, a cui, con cui, in cui); il quale (agreeing, with articulated prepositions) as a formal alternative; il cui + noun = whose (the article agrees with the noun that follows); chi = he/those who (singular verb); ciò che / quello che = what; quanto = all that.
assessment: Uses che for subjects and direct objects and never after a preposition
Uses preposition + cui (di cui, a cui, con cui, per cui) where English can leave the preposition at the end
Replaces cui with the right form of il quale (della quale, ai quali…)
Uses il cui / la cui / i cui / le cui + noun to say 'whose'
Uses chi, ciò che / quello che and quanto correctly

lesson.intro: English can leave a preposition dangling ('the film I told you about') or drop the relative altogether ('the man I saw'). Italian can do neither: the preposition must come **before** the relative, and the relative is never omitted. That makes *di cui, a cui, con cui* essential, and 'whose' becomes the elegant *il cui*.

rules.title: Che: subject and direct object
rules.text: **Che** is invariable and replaces a subject or direct object. It can never follow a preposition. Unlike English, it can't be dropped.

examples.it: Il libro **che** sto leggendo è bello.
examples.en: The book (that) I'm reading is good.

examples.it: La ragazza **che** abita qui è francese.
examples.en: The girl who lives here is French.

rules.title: Preposition + cui
rules.text: After any preposition use **cui**: *di cui, a cui, con cui, in cui, per cui, da cui, su cui, tra cui*. The preposition moves in front: 'the film I told you **about**' → *il film **di cui** ti ho parlato*. *A* can be dropped in formal style (*la persona cui ho scritto*). *In cui* often alternates with *dove* for places.

examples.it: Il film **di cui** ti ho parlato.
examples.en: The film I told you about.
The girl I go out with.
The reason (why) I'm calling you.

rules.title: Il quale: the formal, agreeing alternative
rules.text: **Il quale / la quale / i quali / le quali** agrees with the noun and combines with articulated prepositions: *della quale, al quale, nei quali*. It's typical of formal writing, and useful to avoid ambiguity. It's rarely used for direct objects.

head: cui
il quale (m. sg.)
la quale (f. sg.)
i quali / le quali
rows: con i quali / con le quali

rules.title: Il cui + noun: whose
rules.text: 'Whose' = article + **cui** + noun. The article agrees with the **noun that follows** (the thing possessed), not with the owner: *lo scrittore, **la cui** figlia…*; *l'azienda, **i cui** dipendenti…*.

examples.it: Lo scrittore, **il cui** romanzo ha vinto il premio, vive a Torino.
examples.en: The writer, whose novel won the prize, lives in Turin.

examples.it: È un'azienda **i cui** dipendenti sono molto giovani.
examples.en: It's a company whose employees are very young.

rules.title: Chi, ciò che / quello che, quanto
rules.text: **Chi** = 'the person who / those who', always with a **singular** verb: *Chi cerca trova*. **Ciò che / quello che** = 'what, the thing that': *Ciò che dici è vero*. **Quanto** = 'all that, as much as': *Ho fatto quanto potevo*.

examples.en: Whoever arrives late can't come in.
I don't understand what you mean.
I'll do whatever is necessary.

mistakes.right: La ragazza con cui ho parlato.
mistakes.why: *Parlare con*: the preposition goes before the relative, and *che* can't follow a preposition, so: *con cui*.

mistakes.wrong: Il film che ti ho parlato.
mistakes.right: Il film di cui ti ho parlato.
mistakes.why: *Parlare di* → *di cui*.

mistakes.wrong: Chi vogliono venire alzino la mano.
mistakes.right: Chi vuole venire alzi la mano.
mistakes.why: *Chi* always takes a singular verb.

mistakes.right: Ciò che (Quello che) dici è vero.
mistakes.why: 'What' at the start of a sentence is *ciò che / quello che*.
The article agrees with the possessed noun (*figlio*), not the owner.

tips: If the English sentence ends with a preposition (about, with, for, to), you need *preposition + cui* in Italian.
*Per cui* also means 'so, therefore' at the start of a clause: *Ero stanco, per cui sono rimasto a casa.*
*Il quale* sounds formal in conversation; use it in writing, or when *cui* would be ambiguous.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the correct relative pronoun.
exercises.prompt: Il libro ___ sto leggendo è molto bello.

traps.why: *Il libro* is the direct object of *sto leggendo*, with no preposition: *che*.
*Il quale* is used after prepositions or for subjects in formal style, not for direct objects. Use *che*.

exercises.en: The book I'm reading is very good.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the correct relative pronoun.
exercises.prompt: La ragazza con ___ parlavo è mia cugina.

traps.why: *Che* can't follow a preposition. After *con*: *cui* (or *la quale*).
*Il quale* must agree with *ragazza*: *la quale*.

exercises.en: The girl I was talking to is my cousin.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the correct relative pronoun.
exercises.prompt: Questo è il film ___ ti ho parlato.

traps.why: *Parlare **di** qualcosa*: the preposition must come before the relative: *di cui*.
Only *a* can be dropped before *cui*. *Parlare di* → *di cui*.

exercises.explanation: 'The film I told you **about**' → *parlare di* → **di cui**.
exercises.en: This is the film I told you about.

exercises.prompt: La persona ___ ho dato le chiavi è il portiere.

optionWhy.2: *Di cui* = of/about whom. Here it's 'to whom': *a cui*.
optionWhy.3: *Chi* has no antecedent ('whoever'). Here there's *la persona*.

exercises.en: The person I gave the keys to is the caretaker.

exercises.prompt: Lo scrittore, ___ romanzo ha vinto il premio, vive a Torino.

traps.why: The article agrees with the noun after *cui* (*romanzo*, masculine): *il cui*.
'Whose' = article + *cui* + noun: *il cui romanzo*.
You need the article that agrees with *romanzo*: *il cui*.

exercises.explanation: Whose + masculine singular noun → **il cui** romanzo.
exercises.en: The writer, whose novel won the prize, lives in Turin.

exercises.prompt: L'azienda, ___ dipendenti sono in sciopero, ha chiuso la sede di Bari.

traps.why: The article agrees with *dipendenti* (masculine plural), not with *l'azienda*: *i cui*.
*Dipendenti* is masculine plural here: *i cui*.

exercises.explanation: Agreement with the possessed noun: **i cui** dipendenti.
exercises.en: The company, whose employees are on strike, has closed its Bari office.

exercises.prompt: ___ arriva tardi non può entrare.

traps.why: *Che* needs a noun before it. 'Whoever' is *chi*.
*Quelli che* needs a plural verb (*arrivano*). With *arriva* use *chi*.

exercises.en: Whoever arrives late can't come in.

exercises.prompt: Non capisco ___ vuoi dire.

traps.why: Bare *che* needs a noun before it. Use *quello che* / *ciò che* (or *cosa*).
*Il che* refers back to a whole previous clause ('which'). Here: *quello che*.

exercises.explanation: 'What' = **quello che / ciò che** (or *cosa* as an indirect question).
exercises.en: I don't understand what you mean.

exercises.prompt: Ho fatto ___ ho potuto per aiutarlo.

optionWhy.2: *Cui* needs a preposition and an antecedent.
optionWhy.3: *Che* needs a noun before it (*tutto quello che*).

exercises.en: I did all I could to help him.

exercises.instruction: Join the two sentences with a relative pronoun.
exercises.prompt: Ti presento Marta. Lavoro con Marta da anni.
answers: Ti presento Marta, con (cui|la quale) lavoro da anni

traps.why: *Lavorare con*: the preposition comes first, so *con cui*.

traps.match: Ti presento Marta, (cui|la quale) lavoro con da anni
traps.why: Italian never leaves the preposition at the end: *con cui lavoro*.

exercises.en: Let me introduce Marta, whom I've worked with for years.

exercises.instruction: Replace 'cui' with the correct form of 'il quale'.
exercises.prompt: È una situazione di cui nessuno parla.
answers: È una situazione della quale nessuno parla

match: È una situazione di la quale nessuno parla
È una situazione di quale nessuno parla
traps.why: *Di + la* contracts: *della quale*.

traps.match: È una situazione del quale nessuno parla
traps.why: *Situazione* is feminine: *della quale*.

exercises.en: It's a situation nobody talks about.

exercises.prompt: The town where I was born is very small.
answers: La città (in cui|dove|nella quale) sono (nato|nata) è molto piccola
Il paese (in cui|dove|nel quale) sono (nato|nata) è molto piccolo
La cittadina (in cui|dove|nella quale) sono (nato|nata) è molto piccola

traps.why: 'Where' = *in cui* or *dove*, not *che*.
*Nascere* takes *essere*: *sono nato/a*.

exercises.en: The town where I was born is very small.

exercises.prompt: The reason I'm calling you is simple.
answers: Il motivo (per cui|per il quale) ti chiamo è semplice
La ragione (per cui|per la quale) ti chiamo è semplice

traps.why: 'The reason why' = *il motivo **per cui***.
After *motivo* you need *per cui*.

exercises.en: The reason I'm calling you is simple.

exercises.prompt: He's the colleague I asked for help.
answers: È il collega a cui ho chiesto aiuto
exercises.explanation: *Chiedere aiuto **a** qualcuno* → **a cui**, placed straight after the noun.

exercises.prompt: Those who know the truth say nothing.
answers: Chi sa la verità non dice (niente|nulla)

traps.match: (Quelli|Coloro) che sanno la verità non dicono (niente|nulla)
traps.why: Correct too, with a plural. The task asked for *chi* + singular.
*Chi* always takes a singular verb: *Chi sa… non dice*.

exercises.explanation: **Chi** + singular verb: *Chi sa… non dice niente*.
exercises.en: Those who know the truth say nothing.

exercises.prompt: Ecco il professore ___ figlia studia con me.

optionWhy.1: The article agrees with *figlia* (the possessed noun): *la cui*.

exercises.en: Here's the professor whose daughter studies with me.

exercises.prompt: Tell a friend: 'What you're saying isn't true.'

traps.why: 'What' as a subject = *quello che / ciò che*.
*Cosa* works in questions, not as 'the thing that': *Quello che dici…*

exercises.en: What you're saying isn't true.
